title: Clean code and refactoring
note: Refactoring, in Martin Fowler's sense, changes a program's internal structure to make it easier to understand and modify without changing what it does. Each step is small and checked by tests. A code smell is a surface symptom, such as a long method or duplicated logic, that hints at a deeper design problem.

read.title: Small steps, always green
text: Refactoring is not rewriting. Martin Fowler defines it as changing a program's structure while keeping its observable behavior the same. The method is a series of small, named moves, each followed by running the tests. If a test fails, the last step is small enough to undo or fix immediately. A long refactoring done this way never leaves the code broken for more than a few minutes.

Code smells tell you where to start. A long method is a cue to apply Extract Function, pulling out pieces and naming them for what they do, so the original reads like a summary. Feature Envy, a method that mostly works with another object's data, suggests Move Function to put behavior next to the data it uses. Shotgun Surgery, where one logical change touches many classes, means related logic is scattered and should be gathered.

Names do much of the work. A variable called elapsedDays needs no comment; one called d needs a paragraph. Good comments are reserved for what code cannot say, such as why an unusual approach was chosen or which outside constraint forced it. The aim is code that a teammate can change confidently next month.

o: A failing test then points at a step easy to undo or fix
